rv.q: Were it possible to make an actual reservation at Nell’s West Clare farmhouse, I’d recommend it.
Playwright Erica Murphy explores the cycle of birth and death in an interesting, contemporary fashion.
The Loved Ones offers the pleasures of sharply perceptive writing and acting.
A rare story that incorporates an unexpected pregnancy, fertility issues, and the experience of grief without totally falling into cliché, The Loved Ones is unusually charming.
Now, in Erica Murray’s tender and touching drama The Loved Ones at Irish Rep, Plunkett is playing the bundled-up, buttoned-up Nell, who’s dealing with the recent death of her adult son.
Make no mistake, it's a good night out.

The production, anchored by Maryann Plunkett's grief-stricken Nell, Clare O'Malley's gradual awakening, Alana Raquel Bowers's determined Gabby, and Donna Lynne Champlin's unexpected wisdom, demonstrates what theater can do: it can show us that grace is not the absence of pain, but the choice to stay present in it.
The Loved Ones is a spark of life that ingeniously infuses the importance of shared humanity and the ability to love under seemingly impossible circumstances.
The play’s refusal to veer into melodrama is one of its great strengths, and its power sneaks up on you.

The show’s biggest stumbling block is the introduction of a socially awkward American Airbnb guest (Donna Lynne Champlin), who blunders into the domestic drama with a fruequency and duration that defies common sense — especially on the cramped but cozy farmhouse set (designed by Tatiana Kahvegian and lit by Kat C. Zhou).

cn.t: Critics praise Plunkett's grounded performance and Murray's sharp dialogue in this intimate Irish drama about grief and betrayal, though some find the plot predictable. The ensemble navigates potentially melodramatic material with wit and warmth.

vr.q: This isn't the most dramatic play, but there's a lot to enjoy and I really enjoyed the four performances these women gave. For that, I think it's worth seeing.
